accuracy.evidence: Matched to CCSS 3.MD.C.7a (tile a rectangle with whole-number sides and show the area equals the product of the side lengths) and NC Y4/Y5 area. Every number checked by hand: 4 rows of 6 = 6, 12, 18, 24; 3 × 7 = 21 with 7 + 3 = 10 and 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 as the sum and perimeter; 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 = 15; 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4 (1 × 12 does not fit the 10 by 6 board, so two shapes are asked for); 4 × 3 = 12 doubled to 8 × 3 = 24; 4 m by 3 m = 12 m² with perimeter 14 m; challenge options for 6×4, 5×5, 8×3, 3×7, 9×2, 4×6, 7×5 computed from the same formulas as the correct answer.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented area slips for this stage: adding the side lengths (10 for a 6 by 4, tag add), confusing area with perimeter (20, 14 m, tag perim), counting only the drawn squares when a diagram shows one row and one column (a + b − 1, tag shown), thinking a turned rectangle changes size, thinking a longer side adds rather than multiplies (16 vs 24), and writing cm or m instead of square units (tag unit).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtiles is about the tiling-to-multiplication link itself: rows of unit squares laid into a fixed rectangle with a running 6, 12, 18, 24 count, a part-tiled rectangle solved by choosing a calculation, a rotate button that swaps rows and columns, a corner handle that resizes the rectangle on a 10 by 6 board, and metre squares in a room. flagcover (Understanding Area) covers gaps, overlaps, moving a square and half squares; the lab gate's shingle overlap with every other flagship lab is under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner builds the area one row at a time and sees the count go up in sixes before the text names 4 × 6; picking 7 + 3 or 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 is answered with what those sums really measure; the turn and resize steps make the learner discover that 3 × 5 = 5 × 3, that 3 × 4 and 2 × 6 both give 12, and that doubling a side doubles the area. The step text confirms each rule after the action.

predictions.evidence: Six predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 10 for a 6 by 4 rectangle (adding sides), 'Add the sides: 7 + 3', 'It gets bigger' when turned, 'No, only one can' for area 12, '16: 4 more' for a doubled side and '7 m' for the room.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge rectangles, five of them drawn with only the edge row and column; each wrong option carries a tag (add, perim, shown, unit) whose message names the slip with the actual numbers, e.g. 'You counted only the squares that are drawn. Every row has 8 squares, and there are 3 rows.'

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and the terms unit square, row, area, length, width, cm² and m²; validate_lessons passes the kid and adult readability limits. Adult text names CCSS 3.MD.C.7a and the NC Y4 to Y5 progression and explains why the array makes the formula work.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate clean. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (tile in rows, count in steps to multiply, multiply from one row without drawing all, turning and square units), and each lab step practises exactly one of them; practice and mastery items each test a different slip.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 (dark) and 360 px Android (light) screenshots after Show me on every step: unit squares are about 26 px with readable numbers, the side labels were moved inside the canvas after the first shot clipped '3 m', the resize knob has a 34 px hit radius, canvas cards are about 100 px wide, and the DOM buttons wrap without clipping.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (Lay a row, the three calculation buttons, Turn it, Longer/Shorter/Taller/Less tall, Lay a row of metre squares, 12 m / 12 m²); the canvas aria-label is updated with every spoken result including challenge feedback; walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone.

sources: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3 Measurement and Data 3.MD.C.7a: find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths

Department for Education, National Curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, Year 4 measurement (find the area of rectilinear shapes by counting squares) and Year 5 (calculate and compare the area of rectangles, including using standard units cm² and m²)
NCETM Year 4 and Year 5 area guidance on common errors: confusing area with perimeter, adding the side lengths and using linear units for area
